title: Jaw pain and TMD: when to seek assessment

body:
Jaw pain is common and often settles, but it can also become persistent and interfere with eating, talking and sleep. Temporomandibular disorders, usually shortened to TMD, are a group of problems affecting the jaw joint and the muscles around it.

## What TMD can feel like

Symptoms vary from person to person and may come and go.

- Aching or tenderness in the jaw, face or near the ear
- Clicking, popping or grinding when opening the mouth
- Difficulty opening wide or chewing comfortably
- Jaw feeling stuck, tight or tired
- Headaches or neck tension alongside jaw symptoms

## Why it happens

There is rarely a single cause. Clenching or grinding, stress, previous injury, changes in how the teeth meet and tension in the surrounding muscles can all contribute. The neck and jaw are closely connected, so the two often influence each other.

## When an assessment is worth having

Mild, short-lived jaw soreness often eases on its own. It is worth getting assessed if symptoms continue for more than a few weeks, keep returning, restrict how widely you can open, or affect eating, sleep or work.

## What assessment and management involve

A physiotherapy assessment looks at how the jaw opens and closes, the muscles around it, the neck and posture, and habits that may be adding strain. Management may include advice, relaxation and movement exercises, and neck or posture work where relevant. Sometimes a dentist or GP is also needed, and you can be guided on that.

## Things that may help in the meantime

These are general tips and not a replacement for assessment.

- Choose softer foods while it is sore
- Avoid very wide yawning, gum chewing and nail biting
- Try resting with lips together and teeth slightly apart
- Notice whether you clench during stress or concentration

## Key points

- TMD affects the jaw joint and surrounding muscles
- Many cases improve, but persistent symptoms deserve assessment
- The neck, stress and habits often play a part

## When to seek help

Seek urgent help if your jaw will not close or open, if you have swelling with fever, or if you suspect a fracture after an injury.

This article is general information and is not a substitute for an individual assessment or medical advice.
